knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x^{2} + 1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2 x \\ \text{d}u & =2 x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^{2} + 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{0}^{1}\frac{6 x}{\sqrt{(x^{2} + 1)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x=\int_{1}^{2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{u^{3}}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{1}^{2}3u^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u & =- \frac{6}{\sqrt{u}}|_{1}^{2} \\  & =-6\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+6\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =6-6\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =6 - 3 \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: a*x^n+b>0 throughout closed original x interval; no poles

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =4 x^{2} + 4 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8 x \\ \text{d}u & =8 x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=4 x^{2} + 4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 3 \\ u & 8 & 40\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^{3}\frac{2 x}{\sqrt{(4 x^{2} + 4)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x=\int_{8}^{40}\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\sqrt{u^{3}}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{8}^{40}\frac{1}{4}u^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u & =- \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u}}|_{8}^{40} \\  & =- \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{40}}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}-\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{40}} \\  & =- \frac{\sqrt{10}}{40} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =2 x^{2} + 9 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4 x \\ \text{d}u & =4 x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2 x^{2} + 9.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 0 \\ u & 11 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^{0}\frac{2 x}{\sqrt{(2 x^{2} + 9)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x=\int_{11}^{9}\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\sqrt{u^{3}}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{11}^{9}\frac{1}{2}u^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u & =- \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}|_{11}^{9} \\  & =-1\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}}+1\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11}-1\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =- \frac{1}{3} + \frac{\sqrt{11}}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$
